outcome: Nothing has settled or moved the infinitude question since 26 January 2024. Every source I could open still calls it open or conjectured, the latest base-2 Woodall prime is still the March 2018 PrimeGrid record, and the in-window papers on Woodall numbers (a 2024 Perrin-sequence paper and a May 2026 Padovan/Perrin paper) answer different questions. The only other in-window Woodall-family prime found is a generalized prime in base 355 (April 2025), which is not base 2.
problem_asks: One question: are there infinitely many Woodall primes, i.e. infinitely many positive integers n for which n·2^n − 1 is prime (the standard base-2 definition). Part (a), the only part: the set of n with n·2^n − 1 prime is infinite. The statement does not ask for a density, a bound, a complete list, or a generalization to other bases.

events.what_happened: Wilfrid Keller, 'New Cullen Primes', Mathematics of Computation 64(212), pp. 1733–1741, published 1 October 1995. Per Wikipedia, the paper includes a claim from Hiromi Suyama, told to Keller, that Hooley's 1976 density argument for Cullen numbers can be reformulated for numbers n·2^n + a + b, which would imply that almost all Woodall numbers are composite. A Prime Pages glossary entry, seen only in a search snippet and not opened, reportedly attributes the claim to [Keller95] and hedges it as 'appears to have shown'. The Keller paper itself was not readable (AMS returned 403).
events.delivers: A density statement only: almost all Woodall numbers are composite (the proportion of n up to x with n·2^n − 1 prime tends to 0, as reported). It does not say whether infinitely many Woodall primes exist. The argument is reported as a personal communication, not as a published proof, and the Woodall case is the same argument as Hooley's Cullen case with a and b changed.
events.remains: The whole problem: infinitude of Woodall primes is not addressed.
events.doubts: The Woodall half of the claim rests on a personal communication, not a published argument. Wikipedia reports it secondhand, and a Prime Pages glossary snippet (not opened) reportedly hedges it ('appears to have shown'). The Keller paper's exact wording and any proof sketch were not read (AMS 403), so whether the Woodall case is argued or only asserted is unverified. The result is a density statement and cannot by itself settle infinitude (a logical point; no source claims otherwise).
events.direction: Cuts toward Woodall primes being rare (density zero), not toward their being finite or infinite.
people: Christopher Hooley (1976 Cullen result, which the argument adapts)

sources.supports: the Suyama claim, told to Keller, 'almost all Woodall numbers are composite', and the 1995 date

events.what_happened: Diego Marques and Ana Paula Chaves, 'Fibonacci s-Cullen and s-Woodall Numbers', Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.1.4, published 6 January 2015. For each base s > 1, it gives the explicit form of the possible solutions to F_n = m·s^m ± 1, extending a 2003 result of Luca and Stănică on Fibonacci Cullen and Woodall numbers.
events.delivers: Fibonacci numbers of the form m·s^m − 1 for a fixed base s > 1: finitely many, with explicit form. This is an intersection with the Fibonacci sequence and does not bear on whether infinitely many base-2 Woodall primes exist.

events.delivers: Adds one exponent, n = 17016602, to the known list of Woodall primes. Instances of a question about infinitely many primes; per the scope rule, moves no part of the problem as asked.

events.what_happened: Herbert Batte, Eric F. Bravo and Florian Luca, 'Cullen and Woodall numbers in Padovan and Perrin sequences', arXiv:2605.23084, submitted 21 May 2026 (v1; no later version listed on the abstract page). The abstract states that 1 and 7 are the only Woodall numbers in the Padovan sequence, and that 3 is the only Cullen number in the Perrin sequence. The introduction (HTML) states that 'thirty-four Woodall primes are known'. The HTML rendering shows doubled digits (11, 77, 33); I used the abstract page for the values.
events.revisions: v1 only, 21 May 2026, per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Finiteness of the Woodall numbers in one linear recurrence: only 1 and 7 lie in the Padovan sequence (7 = W_2 is a Woodall prime), and only 3 is a Cullen number in the Perrin sequence. It is a membership result in a different sequence, restricted to Padovan and Perrin, and does not bear on the primality of n·2^n − 1 for infinitely many n.
events.directly_checkable: The finiteness claims rest on a finite search that the authors describe as performed in SageMath 10.6 (per the HTML), not on a formal proof assistant. Anyone can re-run the search with the same bounds.
events.direction: Does not bear on the question. It answers a different question (Woodall numbers inside Padovan). Its only relevance is that its introduction reports 34 known Woodall primes as of May 2026, i.e. no new base-2 Woodall prime since 2018 as far as these authors knew.

disputes.summary: Wikipedia says Suyama told Keller that Hooley's method extends to Woodall numbers, a personal communication printed in Keller's 1995 paper. A Prime Pages glossary snippet (not opened) reportedly attributes the claim to [Keller95] with a hedge ('appears to have shown'). Neither source gives a published Suyama argument. Not a priority dispute.

summary: As of 11 October 2026, every source I could open still treats the infinitude of Woodall primes as open. Wikipedia's unsolved-problems list carries the bullet 'Are there infinitely many Woodall primes?' under Prime numbers (opened at a later offset). The Woodall number article calls it 'an open problem' and the Prime Pages top-20 page says it is 'conjectured that there are infinitely many Woodall primes' (copyright 2026, no update date). OEIS A002234 and A050918, both last modified 11 October 2026, list the same 34 exponents, ending at a(34) = 17016602, with no new base-2 term since the March 2018 PrimeGrid record. The Batte–Bravo–Luca preprint (21 May 2026) also reports thirty-four known Woodall primes. Two in-window papers on Woodall numbers exist: Bravo–Irmak (Turkish J. Math., 2024) on Woodall numbers as Perrin numbers, and Batte–Bravo–Luca (arXiv, May 2026) showing only 1 and 7 are Woodall numbers in the Padovan sequence. Both answer restricted membership questions, not the primality question. The only other in-window results are generalized-base computer finds (Cullen base 69 and generalized Woodall base 355, both April 2025), which are not base 2 and so are discounted. The one older result with real content is Keller's 1995 paper, which reports (via a personal communication from Suyama) that almost all Woodall numbers are composite. That is a density statement, and density zero does not decide infinitude (a logical point; Batte–Bravo–Luca's HTML states Hooley's result only in density terms). I searched for a 2024–2026 density or infinitude argument, a 2025–2026 new Woodall prime, and any AI system's role in this problem, and found none; the AI sweep found AI-driven OEIS and Erdős work (OEIS Open, AlphaProof Nexus, Le Duc–Liberti) but no text in those papers mentioning Woodall or Cullen primes. Close calls: (i) the 2018 record and the 34-prime count are instances, and by the scope rule finitely many instances do not move an infinitude question, so I recorded them but treated them as moving nothing; (ii) the density result could be read as evidence that Woodall primes are scarce, but scarcity is not finiteness, and the sources say so. Discrepancy: a search snippet said OEIS A002234 calls a(34) tentative until 16838832–17016601 is searched, but the OEIS page as fetched has no such comment; MathWorld (which reportedly gives the search coverage) was not opened. Not every source was readable: the Keller 1995 paper (AMS 403), the Prime-Wiki base-2 status page (503), the prothsearch Woodall status page (404), and the Marques 2015 PDF (503 and unreadable binary) could not be opened, so the record relies on their abstracts or on secondary restatements, and the claims drawn from them are marked as such.
competing_reading: Read the 2026 Batte–Bravo–Luca result, the 34-prime count and the 2018 record as movement in the count of known Woodall primes, and read Suyama's 'almost all Woodall numbers are composite' as evidence that Woodall primes are finite. Neither reading survives the question as written: it asks whether there are infinitely many, so finitely many instances move nothing, and density zero does not imply finitely many primes. The strongest case for a different reading is that a Woodall prime found after 2018 and missed in this sweep would change the count; that is an instance-count change, not an infinitude change.
what_would_settle_it: For infinitude: a proof or disproof of infinitude, which no source suggests exists. For the record: the full Keller 1995 text (to see whether the Suyama claim is stated as an argument or a personal communication); MathWorld's search-coverage statement and the PrimeGrid WOO range page (to confirm which exponents have been fully tested and when); the Prime-Wiki and prothsearch base-2 status pages (unreachable now); and the Appendix list of the 44 OEIS conjectures settled in arXiv:2605.22763 (the text read did not include them), which would show whether any concerns A002234 or A050918.

incomplete: Not opened: the Keller 1995 full text (AMS 403), so the exact wording of the Suyama claim and the paper's statement on the largest new Woodall prime are unverified. The Prime-Wiki base-2 page (503), the prothsearch Woodall status page (404) and the Prime-Wiki base-3 page (503) were unavailable, so current search coverage for base 2 beyond the 2018 MathWorld snippet is unconfirmed. MathWorld Woodall prime was seen only in search results. The Marques–Chaves 2015 PDF is unreadable here (binary), so its introduction's statement about Woodall primes is unverified. The Bravo–Irmak 2024 full text (PDF) was not read; I checked the journal page and abstract only, so acknowledgements and any software statement are unchecked, and the first public date within 2024 is not established. The AlphaProof Nexus paper (arXiv 2605.22763): the HTML was read except for its last ~4,000 characters, and its appendix list of the 44 settled OEIS conjectures was not reached in the text, so I cannot exclude a Woodall-related OEIS conjecture among them (the text read does not mention Woodall or Cullen). The AI search relied on the three 2025–2026 AI papers listed above plus snippets from secondary coverage; the seqfan thread, the Lifeboat and Digg headlines, and the autogpt.net and t5k curio claims were not opened and are not relied on. No journal or arXiv version history beyond the abstract pages was checked for the 2024 Bravo–Irmak paper or the 1995 Keller paper.

events.credibility_reason: The Woodall case rests on a reported personal communication from Suyama. The paper itself was not read, and the only other source, an unopened snippet, hedges the claim.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether infinitely many base-2 Woodall primes exist, and no event touches that question. The density-zero claim (almost all Woodall numbers composite) cannot decide infinitude, so it answers a different question and is a variant. It is also a pre-snapshot event. The membership results for Fibonacci, Perrin and Padovan sequences are variants. The two prime finds in base 69 (a Cullen prime) and base 355 are different families or bases, so they are variants. The 2018 record prime is one more finite instance and leaves infinitude untouched. Bravo–Irmak is dated only to 2024, so it gets a null date. The record names no AI system for any event.
judgement.doubts: The AlphaProof Nexus appendix listing 44 settled OEIS conjectures was not read. A Woodall-related entry there cannot be ruled out, though nothing in the text that was read suggests one.
